en: Thus have I heard: the Aggañña Sutta, the twenty-seventh discourse of the Dīgha Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now at that time, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were living among the bhikkhus, desiring the state of a bhikkhu.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion, descended from the mansion, and was walking back and forth in the open air in the shade of the mansion.
In the evening, Vāseṭṭha saw the Blessed One emerging from seclusion, descending from the palace, and walking up and down in the open air in the shade of the palace.
Having seen him, he addressed Bhāradvāja:
"Friend Bhāradvāja, here is the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, descending from the palace, walking up and down in the open air in the shade of the palace."
"Come, friend Bhāradvāja, let us approach the Blessed One;
perhaps we may obtain from the Blessed One the opportunity to hear a discourse on the Dhamma.
"So be it, friend," Bhāradvāja replied to Vāseṭṭha.
Then Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they walked back and forth behind him as he was walking.
Then the Blessed One addressed Vāseṭṭha:

“Vāseṭṭha, you are of brahmin birth, born into a brahmin family, and have gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a brahmin family. I trust, Vāseṭṭha, that the brahmins do not revile or abuse you?”
“Indeed, Bhante, the brahmins revile and abuse us with their characteristic mode of abuse, which is complete and not incomplete.
“But how, Vāseṭṭha, do the brahmins revile and abuse you with their characteristic mode of abuse, which is complete and not incomplete?
“Bhante, the brahmins say this:”
‘The brahmin alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior.
The brahmin alone is the bright caste; other castes are dark.
Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.’
“Brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, heirs of Brahmā.
Yet you, having abandoned the highest caste, have entered upon a lowly caste—namely, that of shaveling recluses, menials, black folk, the offspring of your kinsmen’s feet.

This is not good; this is not fitting, that you, having abandoned the highest caste, have entered upon a lowly caste—namely, that of shaveling recluses, menials, black folk, the offspring of your kinsmen’s feet.”
“Indeed, Bhante, it is in this way that the brahmins revile and abuse us with full and complete abuse, not with incomplete abuse.
“Truly, Vāseṭṭha, it is because they do not remember the ancient tradition that the brahmins say thus:
‘The brahmin caste alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior;’”
‘Only the brahmin is the fair caste; other castes are dark.
Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.
Only brahmins are the legitimate sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.’”
Moreover, Vāseṭṭha, one can see that among the brahmins there are brahmin women who are menstruating, those who are pregnant, those who are giving birth, and those who are nursing.
And yet these brahmins, though born from a womb just like others, say this:
“The brahmin caste alone is the best; other castes are inferior.”
‘Only the brahmin is the fair caste; other castes are dark.
Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.
Only brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.’”
They misrepresent those very brahmins, speak falsehoods, and generate much demerit.
1. The Purity of the Four Castes:
"Vāseṭṭha, there are these four castes—"
Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas.

Now, Vāseṭṭha, even a certain khattiya here may be one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong views.
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, these things are unwholesome, reckoned as unwholesome; they are blameworthy, reckoned as blameworthy; they are not to be cultivated.

Those things reckoned as "not to be cultivated," which are unworthy of a noble one and reckoned as unworthy of a noble one—dark, with dark results, and censured by the wise—are seen here among some kṣatriyas as well.
And so too, Vāseṭṭha, among some brahmins... [and so on].
“Vāseṭṭha, a merchant too...

[and so on] ...a laborer too, Vāseṭṭha, might here be one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view.
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, these things are unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome... [and so on].
Those who are black and have black results are censured by the wise;
even among the *suddas*, some such as these are seen here.
But there is also, Vāseṭṭha, a certain khattiya here who abstains from taking life and abstains from taking what is not given.
He abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter;
he is free from covetousness, possesses a mind without ill will, and holds right view.
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, these things which are wholesome, reckoned as wholesome, blameless, and reckoned as blameless, are to be cultivated.

Those things reckoned as to be cultivated, which are worthy of the noble ones and reckoned as such, which are bright, with bright results, and praised by the wise—some of these are seen here among the khattiyas.
And so too, Vāseṭṭha, [among] the brahmins... [and so forth].
A merchant too, Vāseṭṭha, ...
[and] even a laborer too, Vāseṭṭha, might here refrain from taking life ... [and so on] ...
be free from covetousness, have a mind without ill will, and hold right view.

"Thus, Vāseṭṭha, these things which are wholesome, reckoned as wholesome, blameless, reckoned as blameless, to be cultivated, reckoned as to be cultivated, noble, reckoned as noble, bright, with bright results, and praised by the wise—even some Suddas here are seen to possess them.

While these four castes are thus intermingled in this way, with both dark and bright qualities—some censured by the wise and some praised by the wise—it is in this context that the Brahmins say: [what they have said]"...
‘The brahmin alone is the highest caste; other castes are inferior.
The brahmin alone is the bright caste; other castes are dark.
Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.’
"Brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.
The wise do not assent to this. Why is that?
For among these four castes, Vāseṭṭha, whichever bhikkhu is an arahant— whose taints are exhausted, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done,
laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right gnosis—
it is he who is declared the foremost among them by Dhamma alone, not by non-Dhamma.
For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come.
This can be understood, Vāseṭṭha, by way of this method: that the Dhamma alone is the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come.
King Pasenadi of Kosala, Vāseṭṭha, knows this: [that the Dhamma is the best].
‘The ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a nearby Sakyan clan.
Now, Vāseṭṭha, the Sakyans are subjects of King Pasenadi of Kosala.
They perform acts of humble service toward King Pasenadi of Kosala: they pay homage, rise up for him, join their palms, and show him proper respect.

Thus, Vāseṭṭha, whatever respectful service the Sakyans perform toward King Pasenadi of Kosala—namely, salutation, rising from their seats, joining their palms, and proper homage—the King Pasenadi of Kosala performs that same respectful service toward the Tathāgata:
salutation, rising from his seat, joining his palms, and proper homage; he does not think, "The ascetic is well-born..."
"Gotama, I am ill-born;
the ascetic Gotama is powerful, while I am weak;
the ascetic Gotama is handsome, while I am ugly."
"The ascetic Gotama is of great influence, whereas I am of little influence.
Then, honoring the Dhamma alone, revering the Dhamma, esteeming the Dhamma,
worshipping the Dhamma, and paying homage to the Dhamma, King Pasenadi of Kosala thus performs an act of prostration toward the Tathāgata.
Salutation, rising to greet, joining of palms, and proper respectful conduct.
By this method also, Vāseṭṭha, it should be understood how Dhamma alone is the best among people, both in this visible world and in the life to come.
For you, Vāseṭṭha, have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, though you were of various births, various names, various clans, and various families.
‘Who are you?’— when asked thus, you claim, ‘We are recluses, sons of the Sakyans. Now, Vāseṭṭha,
he in whom faith toward the Tathāgata is settled, rooted, established, firm,
and unshakable by any recluse or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—
It is fitting for him to say:
“I am the Blessed One’s son, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of the Dhamma, created by the Dhamma, an heir to the Dhamma. And why is that?
For this, Vāseṭṭha, is a designation for the Tathāgata: ‘Dhamma-body,’ ‘Brahma-body,’ ‘become Dhamma,’ and ‘become Brahma.
There comes a time, Vāseṭṭha, when after the lapse of a long period, this world contracts.
When the world is contracting, beings for the most part are reborn in the Ābhassara realm.
There they exist as mind-made beings, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, established in beauty, remaining for a long, extended period of time.
There comes a time, Vāseṭṭha, when after the passing of a long interval, this world expands.
As the world expands, for the most part, beings fall from the Ābhassara realm and come to this state of existence.
They were mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, and abiding in beauty; they remained for a very long time, for an exceedingly long duration.
2. The Appearance of the Earth of Taste:
At that time, Vāseṭṭha, the world had become a single expanse of water, and there was darkness, a blinding gloom.
The moon and sun were not discerned; the constellations and forms of stars were not discerned; night and day were not discerned;
months and fortnights were not discerned; seasons and years were not discerned; women and men were not discerned; beings were reckoned only as "beings."
Then, Vāseṭṭha, after the lapse of a long period of time, at some point, the savory earth appeared upon the water;
just as, for example, when boiled milk is cooling down, a film forms on top, even so did it appear.
It was endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, and endowed with flavor; its color was like that of refined ghee or fresh butter,
and its taste was like that of pure, unadulterated honey.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, a certain being who was by nature greedy thought, "Oh, what might this be?
and tasted the earth of flavor with his finger.
As he tasted the earth of flavor with his finger, it delighted him, and craving arose within him.
Furthermore, Vāseṭṭha, other beings, following the example of that being, tasted the earth with their fingers.
As they tasted the earth with their fingers, it adhered to them, and craving arose within them.
3. The Manifestation of the Moon, Sun, and Other Phenomena.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings began to consume the earth-essence by taking it up with their hands in morsels.
And as soon as those beings began to consume the earth-essence by taking it up with their hands in morsels, their own radiance vanished.
When their own radiance had vanished, the moon and sun appeared.
When the moon and sun had appeared, the constellations and the forms of the stars appeared.
When the constellations and the forms of the stars had appeared, night and day became discernible.
When nights and days became manifest, months and fortnights became manifest.
When months and fortnights became manifest, seasons and years became manifest.
To this extent, Vāseṭṭha, this world has evolved again.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings, consuming the earth-essence, subsisting on that and taking that as their food, remained for a long period of time. And as those beings, Vāseṭṭha,
remained for a long period of time consuming the earth-essence, subsisting on that and taking that as their food, so it was for those beings consuming the earth-essence...
Coarseness entered their bodies, and differences in beauty became apparent.
Some beings were beautiful, while others were ugly.
Thereupon, those beings who were beautiful looked down upon the ugly ones, saying:
‘We are more beautiful than these; these are less beautiful than we.
Because of their pride and arrogance regarding their beauty, which was born of such conceit, the savory earth vanished.
When the savory earth had disappeared, they gathered together.
Having gathered together, they exclaimed:
“Oh, what flavor! Oh, what flavor!
Even today, when people obtain something delicious, they say the same thing: “Oh, what flavor! Oh, what flavor!”
‘Oh, what flavor! Oh, what flavor!
Thus they repeat that same ancient, primordial expression, yet they do not understand its meaning.
4. The Appearance of Earth-Crust Mushrooms.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, when the savory earth had disappeared, a crust of earth appeared, just like a mushroom.
It appeared endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, and endowed with flavor; it was as beautiful in color as fine ghee or fresh butter.
"Just as if it were pure, unadulterated honey, such was its flavor.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings set about eating the *bhūmipappaṭaka*.
While consuming it, they remained for a long, extended period of time subsisting on that food and feeding on that."

Vāseṭṭha, as those beings continued for a long period of time subsisting on the earth-crust, feeding on it and making it their nutriment, so to an even greater degree coarseness descended upon their bodies,
and differences in complexion became apparent among them.
At one time beings were beautiful, and at another time beings were ugly.
Thereupon, those beings who were beautiful looked down upon the ugly ones, saying:
"We are more beautiful than they; they are uglier than we."
Because of their pride and arrogance regarding their physical beauty, which gave rise to conceit and overweening pride, the crust of the earth disappeared. 5.
The Appearance of the *Padāla* Creeper: When the crust of the earth had vanished, the *padāla* creeper appeared, just as a *kalambuka* flower appears; even so did it appear.
It became endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, and endowed with flavor; its color was like that of excellent ghee or fresh butter.
Its taste was like that of pure, unadulterated honey.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings set about eating the *padālatā* creeper.
Consuming that, subsisting on that, and feeding on that, those beings remained for a long,
extended period of time. Vāseṭṭha, as those beings remained for a long, extended period of time consuming the padālata,
subsisting on it, and feeding on it, so too did their coarseness increase all the more.
It descended into the body, and a distinction between beauty and ugliness became apparent.
At that time, some beings were beautiful and some beings were ugly.
Thereupon, those beings who were beautiful looked down upon the beings who were ugly, saying:
‘We are more beautiful than these, and they are less beautiful than we.
Because of that pride in their beauty, born of conceit and arrogance, the *padālatā* creeper vanished.
When the *padālatā* had disappeared, they gathered together. Having gathered, they lamented:
‘Alas, what has happened to us! Alas, our prosperity has slipped away!
Even now, when people are touched by some painful condition, they say:
‘Alas, what has happened to us! Alas, our prosperity has slipped away!’”
They merely followed that ancient, primordial expression, but they did not understand its meaning.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, when the *padālatā* had disappeared, rice that ripened without being cultivated appeared; it was without red powder or husk, pure, fragrant, and yielded grains of milled rice.
Whatever they brought in the evening for their evening meal was found in the morning already cooked and grown back again.
Whatever they brought in the morning for their morning meal was found in the evening already cooked and grown back again;
no depletion was perceived.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings, subsisting on that rice which ripened without being tilled, lived for a very long time with that as their food and that as their nourishment.
7. The Manifestation of Female and Male Characteristics:
Just as those beings, Vāseṭṭha, subsisted on that rice which ripened without being tilled, with that as their food and that as their nourishment...
As they remained thus for a long, extended period of time, a further coarseness descended upon the bodies of those beings,
and a difference in complexion became apparent; the female characteristic appeared in women,
and the male characteristic appeared in men.
The woman gazed excessively at the man, and the man gazed excessively at the woman.
As they gazed excessively at one another, lust arose and a fever descended upon their bodies.
On account of that fever, they engaged in sexual intercourse.
But those beings, Vāseṭṭha, who at that time saw one engaging in sexual intercourse threw dust at them, others threw ashes, and others threw cow dung, saying:
“Away with this impurity! Away with this impurity!
“How can one being do such a thing to another being?”
Even today, in certain regions, when a bride is being led away, some people throw dust at her, others throw gravel, and others throw cow dung.
They merely follow that ancient, original expression, yet they do not understand its meaning.
8. Sexual Intercourse.
But what was considered contrary to the Dhamma at that time, Vāseṭṭha, is now considered in accordance with the Dhamma.
And those beings, Vāseṭṭha, who at that time practiced sexual intercourse were not permitted to enter a village or a town for even a month or two.
But when those beings, Vāseṭṭha, fell into the habit of drinking that which is not the true Dhamma to excess, [the situation changed].
Then they began to build houses for the purpose of concealing that very unrighteousness.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, it occurred to a certain being who was by nature lazy:

"Oh, why indeed do I trouble myself, fetching rice in the evening for the evening meal and in the morning for the morning meal? What if I were to fetch rice once for both the evening and the morning meals?"
‘What if I were to gather rice once for both the evening and morning meals?
Then, Vāseṭṭha, that being gathered rice once for both the evening and morning meals.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, another being approached that being; having approached, he said this to that being:
"Come, good being, let us go for rice.
"Enough, good being; I have harvested rice sufficient for both evening and morning meals.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, that being, following the example of the other being, gathered rice sufficient for two days. "Indeed, this too is good, sir," [the first being said].
Then, Vāseṭṭha, a certain being approached another being; having approached him, he said this to that being:
“Come, good being, let us go for rice.
“Enough, good being; I have harvested the rice once for two days.”
Then, Vāseṭṭha, that being, following the example of that other being, gathered rice for four days at once, thinking, “Indeed, friend, it is good even in this way.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, another being approached that being; having approached, he said to that being:
“Come, friend, let us go to gather rice.”
‘Enough, good being, I have harvested the rice for four days at once.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, that being, following the example of the other being, harvested the rice for eight days at once, thinking, ‘Indeed, it is good, good sir, even like this.
And from that time on, Vāseṭṭha, those beings began to consume the rice by means of hoarding.
Then the husk enveloped the grain, and the chaff enveloped the grain;
even when reaped, it did not grow back, and no tracks were visible; the rice stalks stood in dense clusters.
9. The Division of Rice.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings gathered together; having gathered, they lamented:
"Alas, friends, evil states have appeared among beings!
For formerly we were mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, abiding in beauty, and we remained so for a very long time."
After some time, at a certain point in the course of a long period, the earth’s essence appeared upon the water.
It was endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, and endowed with flavor.

We attempted to consume that earth’s essence by taking it up in our hands and making balls of it; as we were attempting to consume the earth’s essence by taking it up in our hands and making balls of it, our own radiance vanished.
When their own radiance had vanished, the moon and sun appeared; when the moon and sun had appeared, the constellations and the forms of the stars appeared;
when the constellations and the forms of the stars had appeared, night and day became discernible;
and as night and day became discernible, the months and fortnights became discernible.
When months and half-months became manifest, seasons and years became manifest.
For a long, extended period, we lived subsisting on the savory earth, feeding upon it and taking it as our nutriment.
But with the manifestation of those very same evil, unwholesome states, the savory earth disappeared.
When the earth of essence had disappeared, a crust of earth appeared.
It was endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, and endowed with flavor.
We then set about consuming that crust of earth.
Feeding on that, subsisting on that, we lived for a very long time.
But with the manifestation of those very same evil, unwholesome states, the *bhūmipappaṭaka* (earth-crust) disappeared.
When the *bhūmipappaṭaka* had vanished, the *padālatā* (creeper) appeared.
It was endowed with color, endowed with fragrance, and endowed with flavor.
We set about eating that *padālata*.
Eating it, subsisting on that, and having that as our food, we remained for a very long period of time.
With the manifestation of those very same evil, unwholesome states, the *padālatā* creeper disappeared.
When the *padālatā* had disappeared, rice appeared that ripened without being cultivated—free from husks, non-powdery, pure, fragrant, and consisting of whole grains.
Whatever we brought for our evening meal would, by morning, have ripened and grown back again.
Whatever we brought in the morning for our breakfast was found in the evening to have ripened and grown back again;
no trace of its removal could be seen.
Thus, subsisting on that rice which required no cultivation, feeding on it and making it our sustenance, we lived for a very long time.
"Because of the manifestation of these very evil, unwholesome states, even the husk envelops the grain, even the chaff envelops the grain;
though it is reaped, it does not grow back, and a depletion becomes apparent; the rice stands in thickets.
What if we were to divide the rice and establish boundaries?"
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings divided the rice and established boundaries.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, a certain being of a greedy nature, while guarding his own portion, took another's portion without it being given and consumed it.
They seized him, and having seized him, they said this:
“Alas, good being, you are doing an evil thing, in that while guarding your own portion, you take and consume another’s portion without it being given.
Do not, good being, do such a thing again! “Very well, sir,” Vāseṭṭha, that being replied to those beings.
And a second time, Vāseṭṭha, that being...
And a third time, Vāseṭṭha, while guarding his own portion, that being took another's portion which had not been given and consumed it.
They seized him, and having seized him, they said this:
“Alas, good being, you are doing an evil thing, in that while guarding your own portion, you take and consume another’s portion without it being given.
Do not, good being, do such a thing again!
Some struck him with their hands, some with clods of earth, and others with sticks.
"From that time on, Vāseṭṭha, taking what is not given became known, censure became known, false speech became known, and the taking up of sticks became known.
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings gathered together; having gathered, they lamented:"
"Alas, indeed, evil states have appeared among beings! For here indeed theft will be known, censure will be known, false speech will be known, and the taking up of the rod will be known.
Suppose we were to appoint one being who would rightly censure him who deserves censure, rightly reprove him who deserves reproach, and rightly banish him who deserves banishment;
and we shall provide him with a share of the rice."
Then, Vāseṭṭha, those beings approached that being who was the most handsome, the most beautiful, the most pleasing, and the most influential among them, and said this to him:
“Come, good being, censure what should be censured rightly, blame what should be blamed rightly, and banish those who should be banished rightly;
we, however, will provide you with a portion of the rice.”

‘So be it, sir,’ Vāseṭṭha, that being replied to those beings. He rightly censured what should be censured, rightly condemned what should be condemned, and rightly banished those who should be banished.
And they presented him with his share of the rice.
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, the first title ‘Mahāsammata’—‘the Greatly Elect’—came into use.
“Because he is the lord of fields, Vāseṭṭha, the second syllable ‘Khattiya, Khattiya’ came into being.
Because he delights others through the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, the third syllable ‘Rājā, Rājā’ came into being.
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, it was in this way that this circle of Khattiyas originated from the ancient, primordial syllable.”

It was for those very beings, and not for others; for those who were similar, and not for those who were dissimilar; and by means of the Dhamma alone, and not by means of what is contrary to the Dhamma.
For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come.
11. The Assembly of Brahmins
Then, Vāseṭṭha, it occurred to some of those beings:
"Alas, friends, evil states have appeared among beings, in that taking what is not given is seen, censure is seen, false speech is seen, the wielding of sticks is seen, and banishment is seen.
What if we were to drive out these evil, unwholesome states?"
They drove out those evil, unwholesome states.
Because they were driving out evil, unwholesome states, Vāseṭṭha, the first term “Brāhmaṇas, Brāhmaṇas” came into being.

Having built leaf huts in forest retreats, they meditated in those leaf huts—free from embers, free from smoke, with pestles laid aside—descending upon villages, towns, and royal capitals in the evening for their evening meal and in the morning for their morning meal, seeking almsfood.
Having obtained that fodder, they again meditate in leaf huts within the forest wilderness.
People, seeing them, said this:
"These beings, sirs, having constructed leaf huts in the forest wilderness, meditate in those leaf huts; they have extinguished the embers."

"Free from smoke and with their pestles laid aside, they descend upon villages, towns, and royal capitals in the evening for their evening meal and in the morning for their morning meal, seeking fodder.
Having obtained fodder, they return once more to their leaf huts in the forest retreats and meditate.
Vāseṭṭha, when it was said, "They meditate," the second syllable, "jhā-yak-ā, jhā-yak-ā," came into being.

Vāseṭṭha, among those very beings, some beings, being unable to achieve that meditative absorption in leaf-huts in the forest wilderness, descend to the vicinity of villages or the vicinity of market towns and remain there making books.
When people see them, they say:

“These beings, sirs, being unable to achieve that meditative absorption in leaf-huts in the forest wilderness, have descended to the vicinity of villages or the vicinity of market towns and remain there making books; they no longer meditate.”
“‘They do not meditate now,’ Vāseṭṭha—thus the third syllable, ‘ajjhāyakā, ajjhāyakā’ (reciters), came into being.
At that time, Vāseṭṭha, they were considered inferior, but nowadays they are considered superior.

Thus, Vāseṭṭha, it was in this way that the ancient, original term for this circle of brahmins arose among those very beings, and not among others; among those who are similar, and not among those who are dissimilar; through the Dhamma, and not through what is contrary to the Dhamma.”
"For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is supreme among people, both in this present life and in the life to come.
12. The Vessas' Circle:
"Now, Vāseṭṭha, some among those very beings, having taken up sexual intercourse as their practice, applied themselves to various crafts."
“Vāseṭṭha, because they adopted the practice of sexual intercourse and engaged in various crafts, the designation ‘Vessas, Vessas’ came into being.

Thus, Vāseṭṭha, it was in this way that this circle of Vessas arose through an ancient, primordial designation—among those very beings, and not others; among those who were similar, and not dissimilar; and by means of Dhamma, and not by means of non-Dhamma.
For Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best thing for people, both in this present life and in the life to come.”
13. The Pure Circle.
"Vāseṭṭha, as for those remaining beings among those very beings, they were of cruel conduct and mean conduct.
Because, Vāseṭṭha, they were of cruel conduct and mean conduct, the designation ‘Suddas, Suddas’ was applied to them."

"Thus indeed, Vāseṭṭha, was the origin of this circle of Suddas through that ancient, primordial expression; it arose from those very beings and not from others, from equals and not from unequals, and by means of Dhamma and not by means of non-Dhamma.
For Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best thing for people both in this visible world and in the life to come.
There was a time, Vāseṭṭha, when even a Kṣatriya, censuring his own Dhamma, would go forth from the home life into homelessness."
‘I shall become a recluse.
And so too, Vāseṭṭha, a brahmin...
[and so on] ...a vaiśya, Vāseṭṭha... [and so on].
Even a Sudda, Vāseṭṭha, having censured his own duty, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, thinking:
‘I shall become a recluse.

Thus, Vāseṭṭha, the manifestation of the recluse-class occurred from these four classes; it arose from those very beings and not from others, from those who were similar and not dissimilar, and by means of the Dhamma and not by means of non-Dhamma.
"For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come.
14. Discussion on Misconduct, etc.
"Furthermore, Vāseṭṭha, even a khattiya, having practiced misconduct by body, having practiced misconduct by speech, and having practiced misconduct by mind..."

Having practiced misconduct, holding wrong views, and undertaking actions based on wrong views, because of undertaking actions based on wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
So too, Vāseṭṭha, a brahmin... [and so forth].
A Vessa too, Vāseṭṭha,
and a Sudda too, Vāseṭṭha,
and even a Samaṇa too, Vāseṭṭha, having practiced misconduct by body, having practiced misconduct by speech, and having practiced misconduct by mind...
Having practiced misconduct, being of wrong view and undertaking actions based on wrong view, because of undertaking actions based on wrong view,
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But a khattiya too, Vāseṭṭha, having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind...
Having practiced good conduct, possessing right view and undertaking actions based on right view, one— on account of undertaking actions based on right view—
upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
It is the same for a brahmin too, Vāseṭṭha …pe…
A merchant too, Vāseṭṭha, ...
a laborer too, Vāseṭṭha, ...
and even an ascetic too, Vāseṭṭha, having practiced good conduct with the body, having practiced good conduct with speech, and having practiced good conduct with the mind...
Having practiced good conduct, possessing right view and undertaking actions based on right view, one— by reason of undertaking actions based on right view—
upon the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination,
a heavenly world. But a khattiya too, Vāseṭṭha, who acts with duplicity by body, acts with duplicity by speech, acts with duplicity by mind, and possesses mixed views...
One who undertakes actions based on mixed views, because of undertaking actions based on mixed views, experiences pleasure and pain after the breakup of the body, after death.
A brahmin too, Vāseṭṭha … [as before] …”
A merchant too, Vāseṭṭha, ...
a laborer too, Vāseṭṭha, ...
and even an ascetic too, Vāseṭṭha, may act with duplicity by body, act with duplicity by speech, act with duplicity by mind, and hold mixed views.
One who undertakes mixed views and actions, by reason of undertaking mixed views and actions, upon the breakup of the body, after death, experiences both pleasure and pain. 15.
Cultivation of the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment.

"Vāseṭṭha, a khattiya too, being restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind, through the cultivation of the seven factors conducive to enlightenment, attains final nibbāna in this very life.
A brāhmaṇa too, Vāseṭṭha … [and] a vessa too, Vāseṭṭha …"
The brahmin too, Vāseṭṭha...

and the ascetic too, Vāseṭṭha, being restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind, through the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment, attains final nibbāna in this very life.
For among these four castes, Vāseṭṭha, whoever is a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, and who has done what was to be done—
"One who has laid down the burden, attained his own goal, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge—
he is declared the foremost among them by the Dhamma alone,
not by what is not Dhamma. For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come."
“Vāseṭṭha, this verse was spoken by Brahmā Sanankumāra:
‘The Khattiya is the best among people who rely on lineage;’”
“Endowed with true knowledge and conduct, he is the best among gods and humans.
Now, Vāseṭṭha, this verse was well-sung by the Brahmā Sanankumāra, not poorly sung; it was well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is beneficial, not unbeneficial; and it is approved by me.
I too, Vāseṭṭha, say this:
"The khattiya is the best among people who rely on lineage."
“Endowed with true knowledge and conduct,
he is the best among gods and humans.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Vāseṭṭhas and Bhāradvājas were uplifted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Aggañña Sutta, the fourth, is finished.
